title: Java 26 performance improvements and garbage collector updates — Complete Guide
description:
Java 26 performance improvements and garbage collector updates — Complete Guide

A practical, in-depth guide to Java 26 performance improvements and garbage collector updates with examples.

INTRO

If you’ve been wrestling with unpredictable latency spikes or excessive heap churn in production, you already know that the garbage collector (GC) is often the hidden culprit. Upgrading to a newer JDK version promises smoother performance, but the reality is that each release reshapes the GC landscape in subtle ways. Java 26 is no exception: it ships with a revamped ZGC, a leaner Shenandoah, and a suite of JIT and runtime tweaks that can shave milliseconds off request times—if you know how to enable and tune them.

The problem isn’t just “old GC is slow.” It’s that most teams keep the default GC settings inherited from Java 11 or 17, missing out on the low‑pause, high‑throughput modes introduced in the last few releases. The result? Higher CPU usage, longer GC pauses, and, ultimately, a poorer end‑user experience. This article teases the most impactful changes in Java 26 and shows why a quick read‑through of the full guide can save you hours of trial‑and‑error in production.

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN

  • How the new ZGC v2 reduces pause times by up to 30 % on large heaps.
  • The Shenandoah “adaptive” mode and when it outperforms ZGC.
  • JIT compiler enhancements that cut warm‑up time for latency‑sensitive services.
  • Practical GC flag combinations for container‑native deployments.
  • How to profile GC behavior with JDK Flight Recorder (JFR) in Java 26.
  • Common pitfalls—like over‑tuning heap size—that can negate the new improvements.

A SHORT CODE SNIPPET 

public class GcDemo {
public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
// Allocate a large object graph to trigger GC activity
byte[][] payload = new byte[10_000][];
for (int i = 0; i < payload.length; i++) {
payload[i] = new byte[1_024 * 1024]; // 1 MiB each
}

// Brief pause to let the GC work
Thread.sleep(2000);
System.out.println("Allocated " + (payload.length) + " MB of data");
}
}

Run the demo with the new ZGC flags to see the difference:

java -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseZGC \
-XX:ZCollectionInterval=500ms -Xmx8g GcDemo

On Java 26 you’ll notice noticeably shorter “Pause” entries in the JFR output compared with Java 17.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

  • ZGC v2 is the default choice for workloads with >4 GB heaps and strict latency SLAs.
  • Shenandoah adaptive mode shines on workloads with frequent allocation bursts and limited CPU headroom.
  • New JIT optimizations reduce warm‑up latency, but they require the -XX:+TieredCompilation flag to stay enabled.
  • Misconfigured heap sizes (e.g., setting -Xmx too close to physical memory) can trigger full GC cycles that nullify the benefits of the updated collectors.

Do Rugby 2023 ao Rugby 2026: evolução da arquitetura Front-End com a CAFFE
description:
Um projeto Front End pode parecer resolvido quando a interface funciona, responde bem e entrega o resultado esperado.

Mas existe outra pergunta que só aparece com o tempo.

Como esse código será compreendido e modificado daqui a dois ou três anos?

Esta é a questão central por trás da evolução do projeto Rugby entre 2023 e 2026.

O Rugby começou como um projeto Front End convencional. Com o passar do tempo, a necessidade de revisitar seu código revelou problemas e oportunidades que não eram tão evidentes durante sua construção.

Essa experiência contribuiu para uma mudança de perspectiva sobre arquitetura CSS e, posteriormente, para o desenvolvimento da CAFFE, CSS Automation For Front End.

Este artigo apresenta essa trajetória.

Rugby 2023: quando organizar significava separar

Na versão de 2023, a organização do CSS seguia principalmente a estrutura visual da interface.

De maneira simplificada, existiam arquivos específicos para o header, hero, banner, cards, footer e outros componentes.

Naquele momento, essa abordagem fazia sentido.

Se o problema estivesse no header, o arquivo relacionado ao header era o primeiro lugar a procurar.

Se fosse necessário alterar o hero, procurava se o arquivo correspondente ao hero.

Era uma relação simples de entender.

Essa forma de organização também ajudava durante o desenvolvimento inicial, porque o código acompanhava a própria composição visual da página.

Não considero essa decisão um erro.

Ela representava uma solução adequada para aquele momento do projeto.

O problema apareceu posteriormente.

O que muda quando revisitamos o projeto anos depois?

Em 2026, ao retornar ao projeto, a perspectiva já era diferente.

O problema não era simplesmente descobrir onde estava o CSS de determinado componente.

Era compreender por que determinada regra estava naquele arquivo e quais outras regras dependiam dela.

Uma alteração aparentemente simples poderia envolver especificidade, ordem de carregamento, estilos globais, containers, tipografia, responsividade, variáveis, componentes e media queries.

A quantidade de arquivos não era necessariamente o problema.

O problema era a relação entre eles.

Isso levou a uma constatação importante.

Um código pode ser organizado para facilitar sua construção e, ainda assim, não estar organizado da melhor maneira para sua manutenção ao longo do tempo.

Fragmentação não é necessariamente um problema

É importante fazer uma distinção.

Separar CSS em arquivos menores continua sendo uma estratégia válida.

O problema aparece quando a fragmentação passa a seguir exclusivamente a estrutura visual da página.

Existe uma diferença entre dizer que determinado arquivo estiliza o hero e dizer que determinado arquivo pertence à camada responsável pelos componentes.

No primeiro caso, a organização acompanha a interface.

No segundo, acompanha uma responsabilidade arquitetural.

Essa diferença se torna mais importante à medida que o projeto cresce.

Rugby 2026: uma nova perspectiva

A nova versão do Rugby não parte simplesmente da ideia de reorganizar arquivos.

A preocupação passa a ser como estruturar o CSS para que suas responsabilidades sejam compreensíveis e previsíveis.

Uma organização conceitual passa a considerar base, layout, componentes e utilitários.

A base concentra reset, elementos e tipografia.

O layout concentra container, grid e seções.

Os componentes concentram header, hero, cards, banner e footer.

Os utilitários concentram espaçamentos, visibilidade e ajustes específicos.

O objetivo não é simplesmente criar mais pastas.

É estabelecer uma relação mais clara entre regra, responsabilidade, camada e componente.

Isso muda a maneira de diagnosticar problemas.

Em vez de procurar apenas pelo nome visual do elemento, passamos a procurar pela responsabilidade arquitetural da regra.

CSS Cascade Layers

Uma das tecnologias que ganhou importância nessa nova perspectiva foi o CSS Cascade Layers.

Através de at layer, podemos declarar explicitamente a organização da cascata.

Por exemplo.

at layer base, layout, components, utilities.

A ideia é estabelecer uma ordem arquitetural entre grupos de regras.

Isso reduz a dependência da ordem física dos arquivos e ajuda a controlar conflitos entre estilos.

A arquitetura passa a participar diretamente da cascata.

Esse é um ponto importante porque muitos problemas de manutenção CSS surgem quando a relação entre regras depende excessivamente de especificidade, ordem de importação, seletores excessivamente complexos e important.

O objetivo não é eliminar a especificidade.

É reduzir a necessidade de utilizá la como mecanismo de arquitetura.

Design Tokens

Outro aspecto importante da evolução foi perceber que determinadas decisões não pertencem aos componentes.

Cores, espaçamentos, tipografia, níveis de z index e estados semânticos representam decisões do sistema visual.

Em vez de espalhar esses valores pelo projeto, podemos centralizá los utilizando propriedades personalizadas do CSS.

Por exemplo, uma variável pode representar a cor principal do projeto e outra pode representar um espaçamento padrão.

Os componentes passam então a consumir essas decisões.

A diferença parece pequena, mas representa uma mudança arquitetural.

Antes, o componente definia o valor.

Depois, o sistema define o token e o componente utiliza o token.

Isso cria uma separação entre a implementação do componente e as decisões globais de design.

A experiência levou à criação da CAFFE

Foi nesse contexto que surgiu a CAFFE, CSS Automation For Front End.

A CAFFE começou como uma tentativa de organizar recursos reutilizáveis para projetos Front End.

Mas a proposta evoluiu.

Hoje, a ideia é trabalhar com quatro elementos principais.

HTML semântico.

CSS arquitetural.

JavaScript comportamental.

Acessibilidade.

A biblioteca utiliza tecnologias nativas da Web e procura evitar dependências externas desnecessárias.

A intenção não é competir diretamente com frameworks como Bootstrap ou Tailwind.

A proposta é oferecer uma base arquitetural pequena, explícita e auditável para projetos que trabalham diretamente com HTML, CSS e JavaScript.

JavaScript e Event Delegation

A mesma preocupação arquitetural aparece no JavaScript.

Uma abordagem tradicional poderia registrar eventos individualmente em cada botão ou componente.

Isso funciona.

Porém, em interfaces maiores, o número de bindings pode crescer consideravelmente.

A CAFFE experimenta uma abordagem baseada em event delegation.

Os elementos declaram seus comportamentos através de atributos data.

O mecanismo central identifica esses atributos e executa o comportamento correspondente.

O fluxo conceitual consiste em um evento no DOM, identificação do comportamento e execução pelo mecanismo da interface.

Isso permite trabalhar com elementos dinâmicos sem precisar registrar manualmente um novo listener para cada elemento criado.

O JavaScript passa a funcionar mais como uma camada de comportamento do sistema.

Acessibilidade como parte da arquitetura

Outra mudança importante está na forma de tratar acessibilidade.

Acessibilidade não deveria ser uma etapa adicionada depois que o componente visual está pronto.

Ela deve participar da arquitetura desde o início.

No desenvolvimento da CAFFE, isso envolve aspectos como navegação por teclado, focus visible, gerenciamento de foco, restauração do foco, Escape para fechamento de elementos sobrepostos, atributos ARIA, tabs semânticas, aria selected, aria current e prefers reduced motion.

Por exemplo, um modal não é apenas uma estrutura que abre e fecha.

Ele também precisa considerar o movimento do foco, a restrição da navegação ao contexto do modal, o fechamento pelo teclado e a restauração do foco após o fechamento.

Esse comportamento faz parte do componente.

Não é apenas um detalhe visual.

O Rugby como laboratório

Nesse processo, o Rugby passou a ter um papel diferente.

Ele não é apenas um site.

Ele funciona como um laboratório de evolução arquitetural.

A relação pode ser compreendida da seguinte maneira.

O Rugby de 2023 proporcionou experiência prática.

A revisão do Rugby em 2026 revelou problemas e oportunidades.

Essas observações contribuíram para a definição de princípios arquiteturais.

Esses princípios foram utilizados no desenvolvimento da CAFFE.

A CAFFE passou então a representar uma estrutura que pode ser reutilizada em novos projetos.

Essa relação é importante.

A CAFFE não surgiu simplesmente porque era necessário criar mais uma biblioteca.

Ela surgiu da tentativa de transformar experiências práticas de desenvolvimento em princípios que pudessem ser reutilizados.

Construir é diferente de manter

Talvez esse seja o principal aprendizado proporcionado pelo projeto.

Quando um sistema está sendo desenvolvido, existe uma grande quantidade de conhecimento na memória do desenvolvedor.

Ele sabe por que determinado arquivo existe, por que determinada regra foi criada, qual componente depende de outra regra, qual solução foi escolhida e qual problema estava sendo resolvido.

Depois de alguns anos, parte desse conhecimento desaparece.

O código permanece.

Por isso, arquitetura também é uma forma de documentação.

Um bom sistema não deveria depender exclusivamente da memória de quem o criou.

Ele precisa comunicar sua própria estrutura.

2023, 2026 e CAFFE

A evolução pode ser resumida em três momentos.

Em 2023, a principal preocupação era construir a interface. A organização acompanhava principalmente os elementos visuais.

Em 2026, a pergunta passou a ser como manter e evoluir a interface. A arquitetura começou a considerar responsabilidades, cascata, tokens, componentes, manutenção, acessibilidade e comportamento.

Com a CAFFE, surgiu uma nova pergunta. Como transformar esse conhecimento em uma estrutura reutilizável?

É nesse ponto que a experiência deixa de pertencer exclusivamente ao projeto Rugby.

Ela passa a alimentar uma biblioteca.

Uma microarquitetura Front End

Por isso, atualmente vejo a CAFFE menos como uma simples biblioteca CSS e mais como uma microarquitetura Front End baseada em tecnologias nativas da Web.

Sua proposta combina HTML semântico, CSS Cascade Layers, Design Tokens, JavaScript Event Delegation e acessibilidade.

A intenção é manter o sistema pequeno o suficiente para ser compreendido e estruturado o suficiente para oferecer previsibilidade.

Não se trata de esconder a Web atrás de uma grande abstração.

Trata se de organizar melhor aquilo que a própria Web já oferece.

O que mudou de verdade?

A aparência da interface não é necessariamente a maior diferença entre Rugby 2023 e Rugby 2026.

A principal mudança aconteceu na forma de pensar o código.

Em 2023, a organização estava diretamente relacionada à interface e aos arquivos CSS responsáveis por cada parte dela.

Em 2026, a organização passa a considerar arquitetura, responsabilidades, componentes e comportamentos.

A CAFFE representa uma tentativa de transformar essa experiência em uma estrutura reutilizável.

Conclusão

Olhar para um projeto antigo não deveria significar simplesmente procurar erros.

Projetos antigos também são registros de aprendizado.

O Rugby de 2023 representa uma etapa importante da minha evolução como desenvolvedor Front End.

A organização por componentes visuais fazia sentido naquele contexto e permitiu que o projeto fosse construído.

Ao revisitar esse código em 2026, entretanto, surgiram novas perguntas.

Como tornar a arquitetura mais previsível?

Como controlar melhor a cascata?

Como reduzir dependências entre estilos?

Como centralizar decisões de design?

Como organizar comportamentos JavaScript?

Como tratar acessibilidade como parte do sistema?

E, principalmente, como construir hoje um código que continue compreensível amanhã?

Essas perguntas ajudaram a direcionar a evolução do Rugby 2026 e também contribuíram para o desenvolvimento da CAFFE.

O Rugby 2023 ensinou sobre construção.

O Rugby 2026 trouxe a perspectiva da manutenção.

A CAFFE representa a tentativa de transformar esse aprendizado em arquitetura reutilizável.

Talvez essa seja uma das principais características da engenharia de software.

Um projeto não precisa ser perfeito quando nasce.

Ele precisa ser capaz de ensinar o desenvolvedor a construir melhor o próximo.

title: JDK in Java
description:
Introduction

JDK stands for Java Development Kit. It is a software package used to develop, compile, debug, and run Java applications.

If you want to create a Java program, you need tools that can convert your Java source code into something the computer can execute. The JDK provides these tools.

For example, when we write:

class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello World");
    }
}

the JDK provides the tools required to compile and run this program.

What is JDK?

JDK (Java Development Kit) is a collection of software tools required for Java application development.

It contains:

  • JRE (Java Runtime Environment)
  • JVM (Java Virtual Machine)
  • Java compiler
  • Debugging tools
  • Other development utilities

In simple words:

JDK = Tools needed to develop Java applications

Main Components of JDK

1. JDK

JDK is the complete development kit.

It is mainly used by Java developers to write and develop applications.

JDK
 ├── JRE
 │    └── JVM
 └── Development Tools

2. JRE

JRE stands for Java Runtime Environment.

It provides the environment required to run Java applications.

JRE
 └── JVM

JRE contains the JVM and Java libraries required for running Java programs.

3. JVM

JVM stands for Java Virtual Machine.

It is responsible for executing Java bytecode.

For example:

Java Code
    ↓
Compiler
    ↓
Bytecode (.class)
    ↓
JVM
    ↓
Program Output

The JVM helps Java achieve its famous feature:

Write Once, Run Anywhere

A Java program can run on different operating systems as long as a compatible JVM is available.

Java Compiler

One of the most important tools in the JDK is the Java compiler.

The Java compiler is called:

javac

Suppose we have a file:

Main.java

We can compile it using:

javac Main.java

This creates:

Main.class

The .class file contains Java bytecode.

We can then run it using:

java Main

JDK Compilation Process

The basic process is:

Main.java
    ↓
   javac
    ↓
Main.class
    ↓
   JVM
    ↓
Output

For example:

Step 1: Write Java code 

class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello Java");
    }
}

Save the file as:

Main.java

Step 2: Compile 

javac Main.java

Step 3: Run 

java Main

Output:

Hello Java

Important JDK Commands

javac

Used to compile Java source code.

javac Main.java

java

Used to run a Java application.

java Main

javadoc

Used to generate documentation from Java source code.

javadoc Main.java

jar

Used to create and manage Java archive files.

jar

jdb

Used for debugging Java applications.

JDK vs JRE vs JVM

JDK JRE JVM
Used for development Used for running Java programs Executes bytecode
Contains JRE Contains JVM Part of JRE
Contains development tools Contains runtime libraries Converts bytecode into machine-level instructions
Used mainly by developers Used to run applications Executes Java programs

The relationship can be remembered as:

JDK
 ↓
JRE
 ↓
JVM

Why Do We Need JDK?

JDK is needed when we want to develop Java applications.

For example, if you want to create:

  • Web applications
  • Desktop applications
  • Backend applications
  • Android-related Java projects
  • Enterprise applications
  • Java-based tools

you need a Java development environment.

The JDK provides the compiler and other tools required for development.

How to Check JDK Installation

After installing the JDK, open Command Prompt or Terminal and type:

java -version

You can also check the compiler:

javac -version

Example:

java version "21..."
javac 21...

The exact version depends on the JDK installed on your computer.

JDK Versions

Java has many versions, such as:

  • Java 8
  • Java 11
  • Java 17
  • Java 21
  • Java 25

Some Java versions are LTS (Long-Term Support) releases.

For learning Java, it is useful to understand that the JDK version determines which Java language features and tools are available.

Advantages of JDK

1. Complete Development Environment

JDK provides the tools needed to develop Java applications.

2. Platform Independent

Java bytecode can run on different platforms using a compatible JVM.

3. Development Tools

It provides tools such as:

javac
java
javadoc
jar
jdb

4. Supports Large Applications

Java and the JDK are widely used for developing large-scale applications.

5. Debugging and Documentation

JDK provides tools that help developers debug programs and create documentation.

Simple Real-Life Example

Think of JDK like a complete workshop for a mechanic.

  • JDK → Complete workshop
  • Compiler → Tool that prepares the program
  • JRE → Environment where the program can operate
  • JVM → Machine that executes the program

Therefore, if you want to build Java applications, you need the JDK.

Conclusion

JDK is an important part of Java development. It provides the compiler, runtime environment, JVM, libraries, and various development tools required to create Java applications.

The most important concept to remember is:

JDK → Development
JRE → Running
JVM → Execution

title: What Screen Readers Actually Announce for a CSS-Only Chart (and Why data-* Isn't Enough)
description:
Good pushback in the comments, worth a proper answer instead of a quick reply, because "store the value in a data-* attribute" is a common instinct that doesn't actually solve the problem.

The core issue

A st-core chart is a handful of <div>s: .chart-fill, .chart-line, .chart-dot, .chart-grid. Visually they're a polygon shape. To the accessibility tree, they're empty, unlabeled <div>s with no text content. A screen reader landing on .chart-fill announces... nothing. Not the shape, not the numbers, not even "chart." It's invisible in the literal sense assistive tech cares about.

Why data-* attributes don't fix this

This is the specific thing worth being precise about. Putting data-value="72" on a .chart-dot does not make a screen reader say "72."

data-* attributes exist for JavaScript and CSS hooks, not for the accessibility tree. Browsers don't expose arbitrary data-* values to assistive tech at all. Two ways people try to route around this, and why they're both unreliable:

  • content: attr(data-value) in CSS — technically renders the value visually via generated content, but screen reader support for CSS generated content is inconsistent across NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver. Some announce it, some skip it entirely, and it's never been part of the reliable accessibility contract. Don't build on it.
  • Reading data-* via JS and injecting it somewhere on interaction — works, but only if you're injecting it into something the accessibility tree actually surfaces (a live region, visible text, an aria-label). The data-* attribute itself is just storage; it does no announcing on its own.

So the value has to end up as real text, or a real ARIA attribute, somewhere in the DOM. That's the actual constraint everything below is solving for.

Two patterns, and when to use each

Method 1 — Visually hidden data table (best for multi-point charts)

The most structured option. A real <table>, hidden from sighted users, fully readable by assistive tech.

.sr-only {
  position: absolute;
  width: 1px;
  height: 1px;
  padding: 0;
  margin: -1px;
  overflow: hidden;
  clip: rect(0, 0, 0, 0);
  white-space: nowrap;
  border: 0;
}

<div class="chart" role="img" aria-label="Weekly revenue chart" aria-describedby="chart-data-table">
  <div class="chart-fill" aria-hidden="true"></div>
  <div class="chart-line" aria-hidden="true"></div>
  <div class="chart-grid" aria-hidden="true"></div>
</div>

<table id="chart-data-table" class="sr-only">
  <caption>Weekly revenue by day</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr><th scope="col">Day</th><th scope="col">Revenue</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td>Sun</td><td>$450</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Mon</td><td>$700</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Tue</td><td>$300</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Wed</td><td>$900</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Thu</td><td>$600</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Fri</td><td>$800</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Sat</td><td>$500</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

Two things doing the real work here:

  • aria-hidden="true" on the decorative divs tells the screen reader to skip them entirely, so it never lands on an empty, unlabeled .chart-fill and announces nothing confusing.
  • aria-describedby links the chart container to the table's id. This is what makes the announcement sequence coherent instead of just "here's a table somewhere on the page, good luck."

What actually gets announced, tabbing through with NVDA or VoiceOver: the chart container reads as "Weekly revenue chart, image" (from role="img" + aria-label), and because of aria-describedby, most screen readers will also read the table's caption right after, or the user can explicitly navigate into it. Once inside the table, standard table navigation takes over, arrow keys or table-specific shortcuts move cell to cell, and each cell reads its column header plus value: "Revenue, column 2 of 2, $900". That's the payoff of using a real <table> instead of a styled list, the semantics come free.

Method 2 — Text summary or live region (best for simple stats)

Overkill to build a full table for a single trend line or one headline number. A sentence does more work:

<div class="chart" role="img" aria-label="Weekly revenue trend, increasing" aria-describedby="chart-summary"></div>

<p id="chart-summary" class="sr-only">
  Revenue rose from $450 on Sunday to a peak of $900 on Wednesday, ending the week at $500, a 12% increase overall.
</p>

One paragraph, one clear announcement, no table navigation required for something that doesn't need it.

Combining both, and handling live updates

For anything with a "Randomize Data" button, there's a wrinkle: updating a table's cells doesn't automatically announce anything, screen readers only speak up on their own when something is in an aria-live region. But making the whole table a live region is a bad idea, every cell update fires a fresh announcement and buries the user in noise.

The pattern that actually works well:

  1. Keep the full data table static (no aria-live). It's there for on-demand navigation, the user tabs in and reads it whenever they want, at their own pace.
  2. Add a separate, short aria-live="polite" summary just for interaction feedback, updated alongside the chart on every data change: 
<p id="chart-live-summary" class="sr-only" aria-live="polite"></p>

function updateChart(values) {
  const style = values.map((v, i) => `--st-p${i + 1}: ${100 - v}%;`).join(' ');
  document.querySelector('.chart-fill').style.cssText = style;
  document.querySelector('.chart-line').style.cssText = style;
  document.querySelector('.chart').style.cssText = style;

  // Keep the full sr-only table in sync too
  const days = ['Sun','Mon','Tue','Wed','Thu','Fri','Sat'];
  document.querySelectorAll('#chart-data-table tbody tr').forEach((row, i) => {
    row.children[1].textContent = `$${values[i]}`;
  });

  // Short, live-announced summary for the interaction itself
  const peak = Math.max(...values);
  const peakDay = days[values.indexOf(peak)];
  document.getElementById('chart-live-summary').textContent =
    `Chart updated. Peak value $${peak} on ${peakDay}.`;
}

Clicking "Randomize" now gets a screen reader user a concise, immediate confirmation ("Chart updated. Peak value $900 on Wednesday.") without forcing them to re-navigate a whole table just to know something changed, while the detailed table stays available if they want to dig in.

The short version

  • data-* attributes are storage, not an accessibility mechanism. They announce nothing on their own.
  • role="img" + aria-label gives a one-line identity to the chart.
  • aria-hidden="true" on every decorative .chart-* div keeps the screen reader from stumbling into empty presentational elements.
  • aria-describedby pointing at a real <table> (or a short <p> for simple charts) is what actually gets the data announced, and gets it announced in context.
  • For live-updating charts, keep the detailed table silent and pair it with a small aria-live="polite" region just for change notifications, don't make the whole table live

title: How to Build a High-Converting Shopify Store Without Writing Tons of Custom Code
description:
Building a Shopify store doesn't always mean writing hundreds of lines of Liquid, JavaScript, and CSS.

The goal is to create a store that is fast, mobile-friendly, easy to use, and focused on conversions.

Here are a few practical ways to do it.

  1. Start With a Flexible Theme

Choose a theme with reusable sections and customization options.

This lets you create:

Custom homepage sections
Product layouts
Promotional banners
Collection sections
FAQs and testimonials

You can make changes from the Shopify editor instead of editing code every time.

  1. Focus on Mobile

Most shoppers use mobile devices, so keep the experience simple.

Consider features like:

Sticky Add to Cart
Easy navigation
Mobile-friendly filters
Fast-loading images
Clear CTAs

Small UX improvements can make a big difference.

  1. Make Products Easy to Find

For stores with many products, good product discovery is important.

Useful features include:

Search
Filters
Sorting
Related products
Product recommendations

Customers should be able to find what they want without unnecessary clicks.

  1. Simplify the Cart Experience

A cart drawer can let customers review their products without leaving the current page.

Useful cart features include:

Quantity controls
Remove options
Upsells
Clear checkout CTA

Keep the journey simple:

Product → Cart → Checkout

  1. Don't Build Everything From Scratch

Before writing custom code, check whether the functionality can be handled by Shopify, your theme, or an existing tool.

For example, Shoptimity provides reusable Shopify sections and widgets for features such as sticky Add to Cart, filters, cart timers, and upsells.

This can reduce repetitive development work while still giving merchants customization options.

  1. Keep Performance in Mind

More features don't always mean a better store.

Always watch:

Image sizes
JavaScript
Third-party apps
Animations
Page loading time

Only add features that actually improve the shopping experience.

Final Thoughts

You don't need a huge amount of custom code to build a good Shopify store.

Use reusable components + Shopify's native features + targeted custom code.

The goal isn't to write more code.

It's to write the right code.

title: New Linux Kernel Flaw Gives ARM64 KVM Guests Read-Write Access to Host Memory
description:
A new flaw in the Linux kernel's KVM virtualization code for ARM64 processors can leave a freed piece of host memory exposed to a guest virtual machine on hosts with nested virtualization enabled.

The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-89775, allows a guest to read and write host kernel memory, and the researcher who found it says it can be used to escape the guest and run code on the host machine.

title: Building a Real-Time Cricket Score App: A Developer’s Practical Guide
description:
Building a Real-Time Cricket Score App: A Developer’s Practical Guide

A live cricket score application is a practical project for developers who want to work with APIs, real-time data, JavaScript, and dynamic web interfaces.

At first, the concept seems simple: get a cricket score and display it on a webpage.

But a useful application needs much more than a single score.

Users may want the current innings, wickets, overs, player performances, commentary, scorecards, upcoming matches, team information, and tournament standings.

The challenge is getting this information into your application efficiently and presenting it in a way that is easy to understand.

A Cricket API can provide the underlying data while developers focus on building the application.

What Should a Cricket Score App Include?

The first step is deciding which features belong in the initial version.

A basic application can start with:

Live match scores
Overs and wickets
Current batsmen
Current bowler
Match status

After the basic scoreboard works, additional features can be introduced:

Ball-by-ball commentary
Detailed scorecards
Player statistics
Team squads
Playing XI
Match schedules
Tournament standings
Fantasy points

Starting with a small feature set makes the project easier to develop and test.

Designing the Data Flow

A simple architecture for a cricket application can look like this:

Cricket API
↓
Backend
↓
Data Processing
↓
Frontend
↓
User

The backend communicates with the external API and prepares the information required by the frontend.

This architecture also gives developers a place to handle authentication, caching, validation, and errors.

Keeping the API key on the server is generally preferable to exposing a private credential in browser-side JavaScript.

Fetching Live Match Data

Once the backend integration is ready, the application can retrieve live match information.

The response might contain information such as:

Match: India vs Australia

Score: 168/4
Overs: 18.2

Current Batter: Player A
Current Bowler: Player B

The frontend can transform these values into cards, tables, or other UI components.

The exact implementation depends on the API response and the framework being used.

Updating the Scoreboard

A live scoreboard needs a way to receive updated information.

One simple approach is periodic polling:

Request
↓
Receive Data
↓
Process Changes
↓
Update UI
↓
Wait
↓
Request Again

The refresh interval should take API limits and application requirements into account.

You don't necessarily need to refresh every part of the application at the same frequency.

For example, the live score may require frequent updates, while a player profile can remain cached for much longer.

Adding Ball-by-Ball Commentary

A scoreboard tells users the current state of the match.

Commentary explains what happened.

A commentary section could display:

18.1 — 1 run
18.2 — FOUR
18.3 — Dot ball
18.4 — 2 runs
18.5 — WICKET

Developers can render these events chronologically so users can follow the progression of an innings.

Combining commentary with the live score makes the match page more informative.

Creating a Detailed Scorecard

The next useful feature is a detailed scorecard.

A batting section could display:

Batter Runs Balls
Player A 72 48
Player B 34 27

A bowling section could display:

Bowler Overs Runs Wickets
Player X 4 28 3

Depending on the available data, developers can also add partnerships, fall of wickets, extras, and over-by-over information.

Building Player and Team Pages

The same cricket data can power pages beyond the match screen.

A player page could include:

Career statistics
Recent performances
Batting average
Bowling average
Match history
Playing role

A team page could include:

Squad
Playing XI
Upcoming fixtures
Recent results
Team statistics

This allows a simple score application to gradually become a broader cricket platform.

Fantasy Cricket Integration

Fantasy cricket applications have another important requirement: player-performance data.

During a match, fantasy points can change as players score runs, take wickets, make catches, or contribute through other match events.

A fantasy dashboard might display:

Player A
78 Runs
94.5 Fantasy Points

Player B
3 Wickets
112 Fantasy Points

The application can use this information to update player rankings or fantasy dashboards.

Developers can keep their own user, contest, team-selection, and leaderboard logic separate from the cricket-data layer.

Handling Errors

Live applications should always be prepared for failed requests.

Possible problems include:

Invalid API credentials
Rate limits
Network errors
Missing match data
Temporary service problems
Unexpected API responses

Instead of leaving the interface blank, provide a useful fallback:

Live data is temporarily unavailable.
Please try again shortly.

Error handling is especially important for live sports applications because users expect the interface to remain usable throughout a match.

Caching the Right Data

Not every piece of cricket information changes frequently.

For example:

Live Score
→ Frequent refresh

Playing XI
→ Occasional refresh

Player Profile
→ Longer cache

Historical Statistics
→ Long-term cache

Using different caching strategies can reduce unnecessary API requests and improve application performance.

It can also help developers stay within API request limits as traffic grows.

Choosing a Cricket API

Before integrating a provider, developers should compare the service against their application's requirements.

Important factors include:

Data coverage
Update frequency
API limits
Authentication
JSON response structure
Documentation
Pricing
Historical data
Scalability

CricLive API provides cricket-data capabilities covering live scores, commentary, scorecards, player statistics, fantasy points, teams, schedules, and standings.

Developers can check the available Cricket API features to see which data categories may fit their project.

Build the MVP First

A complete cricket platform can contain dozens of features, but you don't need to build everything immediately.

A practical roadmap could be:

Phase 1: Live matches and scores

Phase 2: Scorecards and commentary

Phase 3: Player and team pages

Phase 4: Schedules and standings

Phase 5: Fantasy features

Phase 6: Analytics and historical data

This incremental approach makes it easier to test each part of the application before adding more complexity.

Final Thoughts

A real-time cricket application is a combination of data, backend logic, and frontend experience.

The user sees a scoreboard, but behind that interface the application needs to manage changing match information, API requests, authentication, errors, caching, and rate limits.

Using a Cricket API can simplify the data layer and allow developers to concentrate on building useful features around the cricket information.

If you're working on a cricket-related project, you can explore CricLive API and see how its cricket-data capabilities could fit your application.

title: Ophthordle - a new weekly game to test your diagnostic skills!
description:
Ophthordle’s rise signals something important for health-tech builders: diagnostic gamification works because it leverages pattern recognition, feedback loops, and low-friction repetition. What if we applied those same UX principles — not to identifying visual deficits — but to correcting them?

Amblyotube (Meta Quest) does exactly that. Built with WebXR-like rendering pipelines and precise inter-pupillary distance calibration, it delivers asynchronous visual stimuli to each eye while maintaining temporal sync within a consumer VR headset. The result is a lightweight, daily exercise layer over familiar video content—no custom assets or proprietary hardware needed.

This approach trains the brain to integrate inputs from both eyes, improving binocular vision. In amblyopia (lazy eye), the brain favors one eye, suppressing depth perception. Amblyotube provides different visual experiences per eye, enhancing the weaker eye's view while shading the stronger eye's input. This encourages the brain to merge two slightly different images, enhancing hand-eye coordination and spatial awareness.

A central VR control panel lets users adjust Lazy Eye Selection, opacity, blur, contrast, brightness, and gamma. These precise settings are critical; incorrect configurations can worsen imbalances. Once configured, AI-driven logic assigns sharpening effects to the lazy eye and shader effects to the dominant eye, ensuring the lazy eye stays engaged while receiving balanced assistance.

Amblyotube further enhances video content with AI visual processing, making human figures stand out for the lazy eye. A controlled flicker effect draws attention to these figures, leveraging motion and light changes that static exercises cannot replicate. This gamified repetition within enjoyable content creates a potent, low-friction feedback loop.

Integration with YouTube allows users to watch sports, educational, or entertainment content, improving adherence over traditional, often tedious methods. The system’s design leverages the immersive nature of VR to create a focused, yet engaging, therapeutic environment without the need for clinical supervision for daily use.

By using an off-the-shelf platform to deliver structured visual therapy, Amblyotube represents a significant case study in achieving clinically meaningful outcomes through accessible technology. It demonstrates how health-tech can merge wellness, education, and cutting-edge VR to create sustainable user habits. The project is open for developer review, with a public APK available via Seven Sports’ dev portal.

To explore how Amblyotube combines wellness and educational use with cutting-edge VR technology, visit: https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

title: Optimizing Mobile UX: Best Practices for Exceptional User Engagement
description:
Mobile UX best practices are increasingly important as smartphones remain a primary gateway to digital products and services. A mobile experience that is slow, confusing, or difficult to navigate can quickly create friction and affect engagement.

PalTech explores practical approaches in “Optimizing Mobile UX: Best Practices for Exceptional User Engagement”, highlighting how organizations can create more intuitive and effective mobile experiences.

pal.tech

What Makes a Good Mobile User Experience?

Effective mobile UX goes beyond making a desktop website responsive. It requires designing around smaller screens, touch interactions, mobile behavior, and the expectations of users who want fast and effortless experiences.

Key considerations include:

  • Simple and intuitive navigation
  • Responsive and accessible interfaces
  • Fast page and app performance
  • Clear calls to action
  • Touch-friendly interactions
  • Consistent visual design
  • Streamlined user journeys

Why Mobile UX Matters for Businesses

For organizations across the US, Europe, and Australia, mobile experiences can directly influence how customers discover products, complete transactions, access services, and interact with brands.

A well-designed mobile journey can reduce unnecessary friction and help users accomplish their goals with fewer steps.

Designing for Better Mobile Engagement

Mobile UX optimization should be treated as an ongoing process. User behavior, devices, accessibility expectations, and digital trends continue to evolve, making continuous testing and refinement important.

Organizations can combine usability research, analytics, performance monitoring, and user feedback to identify opportunities for improvement.

title: Modern Rust in 2026: What Developers Should Actually Learn
description:
Rust has been around for years, but it still feels surprisingly modern.

It gives you low-level control without forcing you to manually manage memory in the same way you would in C or C++. At the same time, it provides powerful abstractions, expressive types, modern tooling, and a compiler that catches a huge class of bugs before your program runs.

If you're learning Rust in 2026, though, I don't think the best approach is to simply memorize the syntax.

You need to understand how modern Rust thinks.

That means ownership, borrowing, traits, error handling, iterators, concurrency, async programming, Cargo, testing, and good project structure.

Let's explore it.

Why Rust?

Rust is designed around a pretty interesting combination:

  • Performance
  • Memory safety
  • Concurrency
  • Strong typing
  • Zero-cost abstractions
  • Excellent tooling
  • Native compilation

The interesting part is that Rust doesn't use a garbage collector to provide its memory-safety guarantees.

Instead, ownership and borrowing are checked by the compiler.

That sounds intimidating at first.

It is.

But once ownership starts making sense, Rust becomes much easier to reason about.

Rust in 2026: Start With Rust 2024

If you're starting a new project today, Rust 2024 should be part of your baseline knowledge.

Rust 2024 became stable with Rust 1.85.0 in February 2025. It introduced several language and edition changes, including updated lifetime-capture rules, changes around temporary scopes, safer extern blocks, and support for async closures.

The current Rust Book assumes Rust 1.90 or later with:

[package]
name = "my-project"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

The important thing is that an edition isn't simply a completely new language version.

Rust editions provide a way to introduce changes while maintaining compatibility across the ecosystem.

Getting Started

If you don't have Rust installed, rustup is the standard toolchain manager.

Check your installation:

rustc --version
cargo --version
rustup --version

Create a project:

cargo new hello-rust
cd hello-rust

Run it:

cargo run

You'll get the classic:

Hello, world!

But Cargo is much more than a command that runs your application.

It becomes the center of your Rust workflow.

Learn Cargo Early

These commands are worth memorizing:

cargo check
cargo build
cargo run
cargo test
cargo fmt
cargo clippy

I particularly recommend getting comfortable with:

cargo check

It lets you quickly verify whether your code compiles without always producing the final executable.

Then:

cargo clippy

can help identify suspicious or non-idiomatic code.

And:

cargo fmt

keeps formatting consistent.

A simple development loop can therefore become:

cargo fmt
cargo check
cargo clippy
cargo test

This is one of the reasons Rust's tooling feels so cohesive.

Ownership Is the Big One

If you're coming from JavaScript, Python, Java, or another garbage-collected language, ownership is probably going to be the biggest mental shift.

Consider:

fn main() {
    let name = String::from("Charlie");

    let other_name = name;

    println!("{other_name}");
}

Here:

let other_name = name;

moves ownership of the String.

The original name can no longer be used as if it still owned the value.

Why?

Because Rust needs to know exactly who is responsible for the data.

This ownership model is one of the foundations of Rust's memory-safety guarantees.

Borrow Instead of Moving

You don't always need to transfer ownership.

You can borrow:

fn print_name(name: &str) {
    println!("{name}");
}

fn main() {
    let name = String::from("Charlie");

    print_name(&name);

    println!("{name}");
}

The function receives a reference rather than taking ownership.

This is where Rust starts becoming interesting.

Instead of relying on a garbage collector to figure out memory usage later, the compiler checks the ownership relationships while you're writing the program.

Mutable Borrowing

Rust also controls mutable access.

fn add_exclamation(message: &mut String) {
    message.push('!');
}

fn main() {
    let mut message = String::from("Hello");

    add_exclamation(&mut message);

    println!("{message}");
}

The &mut tells Rust that the function is borrowing the value mutably.

Rust's borrowing rules prevent conflicting accesses that could otherwise result in memory bugs.

Don't Fear Lifetimes

Eventually you'll encounter something like:

fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if a.len() > b.len() {
        a
    } else {
        b
    }
}

This is a lifetime annotation.

The important thing is not to start by memorizing every lifetime rule.

Think of a lifetime as describing the relationship between references.

Rust uses this information to verify that references don't outlive the data they're referring to.

And in many situations, Rust can infer lifetimes for you.

Traits Are One of Rust's Superpowers

If you're coming from object-oriented programming, Rust's traits may initially feel different.

A trait defines behavior.

trait Speak {
    fn speak(&self);
}

A type can implement that behavior:

struct Dog;

impl Speak for Dog {
    fn speak(&self) {
        println!("Woof!");
    }
}

Now we can use the trait as an abstraction.

Traits become even more powerful when combined with generics:

fn make_it_speak<T: Speak>(animal: &T) {
    animal.speak();
}

This is one of the areas where Rust's type system becomes extremely expressive.

Generics Without Giving Up Performance

Rust lets you write generic code without necessarily paying the runtime cost associated with dynamic dispatch.

For example:

fn print_value<T: std::fmt::Display>(value: T) {
    println!("{value}");
}

You can make this more readable with a where clause:

fn print_value<T>(value: T)
where
    T: std::fmt::Display,
{
    println!("{value}");
}

As your trait bounds become more complicated, where clauses can make APIs much easier to understand.

Enums Are Much More Than Constants

Rust enums can contain data.

enum Message {
    Text(String),
    Number(i32),
    Quit,
}

Then you can use pattern matching:

fn handle(message: Message) {
    match message {
        Message::Text(text) => println!("Text: {text}"),
        Message::Number(number) => println!("Number: {number}"),
        Message::Quit => println!("Quit"),
    }
}

This becomes incredibly useful for modeling application state.

For example:

enum ConnectionState {
    Connecting,
    Connected,
    Disconnected,
    Failed(String),
}

Instead of passing around strings like:

"connected"
"failed"
"disconnected"

you can make the possible states explicit in the type system.

Option<T> Instead of Null

Rust doesn't use null as its standard mechanism for missing values.

Instead, you get:

Option<T>

which can contain:

Some(value)

or:

None

For example:

fn find_username(id: u64) -> Option<String> {
    if id == 1 {
        Some("Charlie".into())
    } else {
        None
    }
}

Then:

match find_username(1) {
    Some(name) => println!("User: {name}"),
    None => println!("User not found"),
}

The compiler makes the possibility of "no value" explicit.

Result<T, E> for Errors

Rust also makes errors explicit.

Instead of silently returning a special value, a function can return:

Result<T, E>

For example:

fn divide(a: f64, b: f64) -> Result<f64, String> {
    if b == 0.0 {
        Err("Cannot divide by zero".into())
    } else {
        Ok(a / b)
    }
}

Then:

match divide(10.0, 2.0) {
    Ok(result) => println!("{result}"),
    Err(error) => println!("Error: {error}"),
}

This is one of the patterns you'll use constantly in real Rust applications.

The ? Operator Makes Error Handling Better

Imagine having to manually propagate every error:

match load_config() {
    Ok(config) => config,
    Err(error) => return Err(error),
}

Rust gives you a much cleaner option:

let config = load_config()?;

You can chain operations:

fn start_application() -> Result<(), AppError> {
    let config = load_config()?;
    let database = connect_database(&config)?;
    start_server(database)?;

    Ok(())
}

This style keeps the happy path readable while still propagating errors correctly.

Iterators Are Worth Learning

Rust's iterator system is one of the places where the language feels very modern.

Instead of:

let mut result = Vec::new();

for number in numbers {
    if number % 2 == 0 {
        result.push(number * 2);
    }
}

you can write:

let result: Vec<_> = numbers
    .into_iter()
    .filter(|n| n % 2 == 0)
    .map(|n| n * 2)
    .collect();

This style can make data transformations much easier to read.

And because iterators are lazy, operations such as filter and map can form a pipeline rather than immediately creating intermediate collections.

Concurrency Without Garbage-Collector Magic

Rust's ownership and type systems also play a major role in concurrent programming.

A basic thread:

use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let handle = thread::spawn(|| {
        println!("Hello from another thread!");
    });

    handle.join().unwrap();
}

For shared state, you might encounter:

Arc<Mutex<T>>

For example:

use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let counter = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0));

    let mut handles = Vec::new();

    for _ in 0..4 {
        let counter = Arc::clone(&counter);

        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            let mut value = counter.lock().unwrap();
            *value += 1;
        }));
    }

    for handle in handles {
        handle.join().unwrap();
    }

    println!("{}", *counter.lock().unwrap());
}

Rust's ownership and type systems are designed to prevent many classes of concurrency bugs at compile time.

But Don't Reach for Arc<Mutex<T>> Immediately

This is an important practical lesson.

When the compiler makes shared state difficult, your first response shouldn't always be:

Arc<Mutex<_>>

Ask:

Who should own this data?

Then:

Who actually needs access to it?

Then:

Does that access really need to be mutable?

Sometimes a channel or a better ownership design is much cleaner than shared mutable state.

Rust often pushes you toward better architecture.

Async Rust

Async Rust is a major part of modern Rust development.

The basic syntax looks familiar:

async fn fetch_data() {
    // async work
}

and:

let result = fetch_data().await;

But there's an important detail:

Rust does not ship with one built-in async runtime.

Async functions produce futures, and an async runtime is responsible for executing those futures.

The Rust Book explains that async/await builds on the Future trait and that async code needs a runtime to actually execute those futures.

This is why ecosystems such as Tokio are so important in practical async Rust applications.

Futures, Pin, and Poll

If you're going deeper into async Rust, you'll eventually encounter:

Future
Pin
Poll
Waker

At first, this can look terrifying.

You don't need to understand every internal detail before building an async application.

But understanding the basic model helps.

An async function is transformed into a future representing work that may be suspended and resumed. Rust's compiler and async machinery maintain the ownership and borrowing guarantees across those suspension points.

You can start with:

async/await

and later explore:

Future
   ↓
Poll
   ↓
Waker
   ↓
Executor

when you need deeper control.

Async Closures

One of the notable Rust 2024 additions is support for async closures:

let fetch = async || {
    // async work
};

Rust 1.85 stabilized async closures alongside the 2024 Edition.

This is useful when you need closures that themselves perform asynchronous operations.

Send and Sync

When working with threads and async runtimes, two traits appear frequently:

Send
Sync

A simplified way to think about them is:

Send: a value can be transferred between threads safely.

Sync: references to a value can be shared between threads safely.

You don't usually need to implement these traits manually.

Instead, Rust determines whether your types satisfy the requirements based on the types they contain.

Once you start building multi-threaded or async applications, understanding these two traits becomes increasingly important.

Smart Pointers

Rust provides several smart-pointer types.

Some important ones are:

Box<T>
Rc<T>
Arc<T>
Cell<T>
RefCell<T>
Mutex<T>
RwLock<T>

For example:

let value = Box::new(42);

For shared ownership in single-threaded code:

use std::rc::Rc;

let value = Rc::new(String::from("hello"));

let a = Rc::clone(&value);
let b = Rc::clone(&value);

For shared ownership across threads:

use std::sync::Arc;

let value = Arc::new(String::from("hello"));

let copy = Arc::clone(&value);

The important part isn't memorizing all of these.

It's understanding why you need one.

Unsafe Rust

Rust isn't completely "unsafe-free."

It gives you an explicit boundary:

unsafe {
    // unsafe operations
}

Unsafe Rust may be necessary for:

  • FFI
  • Hardware access
  • Operating-system interfaces
  • Raw pointers
  • Low-level optimizations
  • Custom memory management

The goal isn't to eliminate unsafe code entirely.

The goal is to keep unsafe code contained and build safe abstractions around it.

Don't Use clone() to Silence the Compiler

This is probably one of the most useful lessons for beginners.

You write:

let copy = value.clone();

and suddenly the compiler stops complaining.

Problem solved?

Maybe.

But maybe you've just hidden an ownership problem.

Sometimes cloning is exactly what you want.

Sometimes you should borrow:

fn process(data: &Data) {
    // ...
}

Before adding .clone(), ask:

Do I actually need another owned copy?

If the answer is no, a reference may be the better design.

Don't Use unwrap() Everywhere

During experimentation, this is perfectly normal:

let value = operation().unwrap();

But production code needs more thought.

Instead:

let value = operation()?;

or:

match operation() {
    Ok(value) => process(value),
    Err(error) => handle_error(error),
}

unwrap() isn't inherently bad.

It just means:

"I believe this cannot fail here."

Make sure that statement is actually true.

Testing

Rust has built-in testing support.

fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
    a + b
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn addition_works() {
        assert_eq!(add(2, 3), 5);
    }
}

Run:

cargo test

You can also put executable examples in documentation, allowing code examples to be checked as part of your testing workflow.

This is particularly useful when developing libraries.

Clippy + Rustfmt

Two tools I recommend using from the beginning:

cargo fmt

and:

cargo clippy

rustfmt handles formatting.

Clippy provides additional lints that can catch common mistakes and encourage idiomatic Rust.

Your CI pipeline can therefore include:

cargo fmt --check
cargo clippy
cargo test

That's a very reasonable baseline for a Rust project.

A Practical Rust Project Structure

For a small project:

my-app/
├── Cargo.toml
└── src/
    └── main.rs

is completely fine.

Don't create a massive architecture before you have a problem to solve.

As the project grows:

my-app/
├── Cargo.toml
├── src/
│   ├── main.rs
│   ├── config.rs
│   ├── error.rs
│   ├── models.rs
│   ├── services.rs
│   └── api/
│       ├── mod.rs
│       └── users.rs
└── tests/

can make sense.

For larger systems, Cargo workspaces can separate applications and libraries into multiple crates.

Rust for Backend Development

Rust is a strong option for backend systems where performance, resource efficiency, and correctness matter.

You can use it for:

  • REST APIs
  • WebSockets
  • Networking
  • Authentication
  • Microservices
  • Database services
  • Infrastructure

A typical architecture might look like:

Client
   |
   v
API
   |
   +---- Authentication
   |
   +---- Business Logic
   |
   +---- Database
   |
   +---- Cache
   |
   +---- External Services

Async Rust becomes especially useful when your application spends significant time waiting on I/O.

Rust for CLI Tools

Rust is also excellent for command-line applications.

You get:

  • Native binaries
  • Fast startup
  • Strong error handling
  • Cross-platform support
  • Excellent dependency management

This makes Rust a particularly interesting choice for developer tooling.

Rust for Embedded Systems

If you're interested in electronics, robotics, or embedded systems, Rust becomes even more interesting.

Rust can be used for:

  • Microcontrollers
  • Sensors
  • Robotics
  • IoT
  • Hardware interfaces
  • Automotive systems
  • Low-level firmware

The combination of low-level control and compile-time safety makes it worth exploring for embedded development.

What Should You Actually Learn?

Don't try to learn everything at once.

I'd approach modern Rust in roughly this order:

Level 1 — Fundamentals

Learn:

Variables
Functions
Structs
Enums
Pattern matching
Collections
Ownership
Borrowing

Level 2 — Type System

Then:

Generics
Traits
Trait bounds
Lifetimes
Option
Result
Error handling

Level 3 — Idiomatic Rust

Then:

Iterators
Closures
Modules
Smart pointers
Testing
Documentation
Cargo
Clippy
Rustfmt

Level 4 — Advanced Rust

Then:

Concurrency
Async/await
Future
Send
Sync
Pin
Channels
Macros
Unsafe Rust
FFI

Level 5 — Build Something

This is the important part.

Build:

  • A CLI tool
  • A REST API
  • A TCP server
  • A file-processing application
  • A database-backed service
  • An embedded project
  • A WebAssembly application

You learn Rust much faster when the compiler is complaining about a real project rather than a tutorial exercise.

A Small Example Combining Modern Rust Concepts

Here's a small example using structs, borrowing, iterators, and filtering:

#[derive(Debug)]
struct User {
    name: String,
    age: u32,
}

fn adult_users(users: &[User]) -> Vec<&User> {
    users
        .iter()
        .filter(|user| user.age >= 18)
        .collect()
}

fn main() {
    let users = vec![
        User {
            name: "Alice".into(),
            age: 20,
        },
        User {
            name: "Bob".into(),
            age: 16,
        },
    ];

    let adults = adult_users(&users);

    for user in adults {
        println!("{user:?}");
    }
}

It's a small program, but look at how many Rust concepts are already involved:

  • Structs
  • Ownership
  • Borrowing
  • Slices
  • References
  • Iterators
  • Closures
  • Type inference

That's why Rust can feel difficult initially.

There are a lot of concepts interacting with each other.

But that's also what makes the language powerful.

My Biggest Rust Tip

Don't try to "beat" the borrow checker.

Work with it.

When Rust gives you an error, don't immediately add:

.clone()
Arc
Mutex
RefCell
unsafe

Instead, stop and ask:

Who owns this data?

Who needs it?

Does that code need to modify it?

How long does the reference actually need to live?

Those questions often lead to a much cleaner solution.

Final Thoughts

Modern Rust isn't just about writing fast code.

It's about making the relationships inside your program explicit.

Who owns the data?

Who can modify it?

What happens when something fails?

Can two threads access this safely?

Can this reference outlive the data?

What should happen when a value doesn't exist?

Rust makes you answer these questions early.

At first, that can feel annoying.

Later, it starts feeling like one of the language's biggest advantages.

If you're starting Rust in 2026, don't focus only on syntax.

Learn the mental model.

Start with ownership and borrowing.

Then move into traits, enums, Result, iterators, concurrency, async Rust, and the tooling around Cargo.

And most importantly:

Build things.

The compiler isn't your enemy.

Let it teach you.

What's Next?

If you're exploring software development alongside Rust, you can also check out my web development work:

Ajnas Ahammed — Web Development

Keep building, keep breaking things, and keep learning.

That's how you get better at programming.

title: The variance problem in AI products
description:
Users forgive a slow answer. What breaks trust is an AI product that is fast one day, slow the next, and never says why.

Quick note: I wrote this article from firsthand experience as a founder and engineer. I co-build browser tools that run on top of several of the AI chat products mentioned here. I have no relationship with the companies that make them.

A transcription product ships. On a short clip, the result comes back in two seconds. A week later, the same user records a longer passage and waits six seconds, which is exactly how long a passage that size takes. They assume it is broken.

That story is not mine. It came from Bilal Skiani, who builds a transcription product called Genie 007 and shared it in the comments of an earlier piece of mine on waiting in AI interfaces. Nothing about the system changed between the two runs. What changed was the user’s reference point. The two-second run set the promise, and the six-second run broke it. As Bilal put it in that thread: “Variance isn’t the trust killer, unexplained variance is.”

AI products produce more of this than any software category before them. The same prompt can take one second or forty, depending on model load, reasoning depth, tool calls and input length. Most products respond to that variance in one of two ways, and both are wrong.

The fastest answer becomes the promise

Users do not judge an AI product by its average response time. They judge it against the fastest response they have personally seen. Tversky and Kahneman described the mechanism in 1974: people estimate by starting from an initial value and adjusting, and the adjustment is usually too small (Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases). In an interface, the first fast result is that initial value.

I see the same pattern in the tools I work on. Search and export on a small history finish almost instantly. When the same operation runs on a large history and takes longer, the support messages change character. They stop asking “how do I use this” and start asking “is this broken”. Same code, same architecture, different input size.

This is why “it’s usually fast” is not a defence. The snappy case earns goodwill that the slow case then spends, and the product never gets to choose which case the user remembers.

Two common answers, and why both fail

AI products currently handle variance by either exposing it raw or flattening it with an artificial floor, and each trades one failure for another. Raw variance means a spinner and a word like “Thinking” that looks identical at one second and at forty. The user has no way to tell a long job from a stuck one.

The floor is subtler. Some teams add a minimum delay so fast responses never set an unrealistic anchor. It works, in the narrow sense that slow runs stop feeling broken. But it erases the upside to prevent one kind of downside. Every fast answer the system could have given is now deliberately slowed, forever, to protect the user from a comparison the interface could have explained instead.

Both approaches treat variance as the problem. It is not. David Maister named the actual problem in 1985, writing about queues rather than software: “Unexplained Waits Are Longer than Explained Waits”, and “Uncertain Waits Are Longer than Known, Finite Waits” (The Psychology of Waiting Lines). A variable wait is fine. An unexplained variable wait is the one that feels broken.

The question has moved from whether to show progress to what it should say

Progress indicators are at the point error messages reached decades ago: nobody argues about whether to show one anymore, and the open question is what it should tell the user. The research to answer it has existed for a long time.

Brad Myers found in 1985 that users strongly prefer interfaces with percent-done progress indicators (The importance of percent-done progress indicators). Jakob Nielsen’s first usability heuristic asks that the design “always keep users informed about what is going on” (10 Usability Heuristics). Bruce Tognazzini lists “Keep users informed when they face delay” among his principles of latency reduction, alongside a separate principle of anticipation (First Principles of Interaction Design). Chris Harrison and colleagues later found that the behaviour of a progress bar changes how long the same wait feels (Rethinking the progress bar).

The most useful line for AI teams, though, is from Nielsen’s essay on response times, and it covers exactly the case where a system cannot know how long it will take: “a system searching an unknown number of remote databases could print the name of each database as it is processed.” A spinner, he adds, is “a last resort”, because it “does not indicate what it is doing” (Response Times: The 3 Important Limits).

Build pipelines are the cleanest non-AI example of this gap. Every command, exit code and timestamp is recorded. The status the person actually looks at is a spinner and the word “Running”. The technical problem is solved. The editorial one is not, and it is the same gap AI products have.

Name the work, not the clock

When an AI product cannot bound how long something will take, it should say what it is doing rather than how long it will take. There are two kinds of anticipation, and Bilal’s distinction between them is sharper than anything I had written before.

Time anticipation, “this takes about 10 seconds”, makes a promise about duration, so it breaks the moment reality overshoots. Process anticipation, “scanning your conversation history”, names the work. The user’s anchor sits on the work instead of the clock, so a longer run does not break a contract, because no contract about time was offered.

There is an honesty argument underneath the usability one. A time estimate is a best guess dressed as a promise. A process description is a true statement about what is happening right now. Users sense the difference over repeated use, even when they cannot name it. As Bilal put it: “One estimate being off reads as noise. A pattern reads as a character flaw.”

Some shipped AI products already do this in small ways. Anthropic’s help centre, describing how Claude handles long conversations, says: “You may occasionally see that Claude is ‘organizing its thoughts’ during long conversations”, and explains that the message means automatic context management is working (Anthropic Help Center). It names a process and promises no duration. The wording is anthropomorphic rather than literal, which is a separate debate, but the structure is the right one.

My working heuristic for when a time estimate is still acceptable, offered as a practitioner’s read rather than a study: if the worst case stays under roughly twice the estimate, “about 10 seconds” survives a 15 or 18 second run. Past about 20 it starts to bite, and past 25 it becomes a liability. If you cannot bound the worst case, do not say a number. Name the work.

A description that lies is worse than a spinner

A progress message that describes the wrong thing does more damage than a missed time estimate, because it gives the user a false model of the system that they carry into every later interaction. “Analyzing your document”, shown while the system is actually waiting on a slow network call, is not imprecise. It is fiction.

Bilal described exactly this in an earlier version of his own product. Its progress messages rotated on a timer, regardless of what the system was doing. It looked clean in demos. In production there were cases where the model finished in about 400 milliseconds while the interface was still cycling through “processing your request”, because the rotation was bound to time, not to state. The user waited for nothing.

The discipline test is simple: does the visible description change when the underlying operation changes? If it does not survive a real change of state without lying, it is narrative cover, not reporting. There is a cheap way to pass the test, tagging each major operation with its own description and switching the visible one as the system moves, and an expensive way, deriving the description from live telemetry. The trap is the third option most teams ship: descriptions written once and deployed, which look like reporting and are not.

This is also an organisational problem, not only a design one. Descriptions written once usually come from someone who is not building the state machine. The fix requires the person writing the words to know what the system actually does, which in practice means the writer and the builder sit together, or are the same person.

Trust degrades quietly, then suddenly

Latency has a dashboard and accuracy has a benchmark, but trust degradation has neither, which is why teams find out about it late. Bilal’s line for this is the one I have repeated most since: “Latency degrades loudly. Trust degrades quietly, then suddenly.”

Most failure modes in software are roughly proportional. Latency rises with load. Errors rise with bad inputs. Trust does not behave that way. It erodes one unexplained wait at a time, and then collapses around some unrelated trigger. By the time retention or ratings move, the decision to leave was made weeks earlier.

That puts process honesty in the same category as accessibility and security. All three have to be designed in rather than added on, all three are usually retrofitted by people who did not make the original decisions, and all three stay invisible until something breaks. For trust, the thing that breaks is usually a support thread or a slow drift in a retention curve.

The practical response is to own at least one leading indicator for trust rather than waiting for lagging ones. Watch session recordings for users opening a second tab to check whether something is still working. Track the kind of support question people ask, not only the number. Those shifts show up months before churn does.

Where to start

If a team can ship only one thing, it should ship anticipation before real-time feedback. A single sentence that sets the anchor before the wait, naming the work rather than the time, can be owned end to end by one person, and it sets the reference point before the user forms their own. Real-time feedback has to fight an anchor that already exists.

The second step is coupling: bind each description to the state it describes, so the words change when the work changes. The third is measurement: decide how you will notice trust eroding before a retention chart tells you.

None of this requires removing variance. AI systems will keep being fast sometimes and slow other times. What users need is a product that tells them which one is happening, in words that stay true while it happens. Or, as Bilal said when we discussed how much of this a small team can realistically build: “A shipped sentence beats a coordinated system that never ships.”

Thanks to Bilal Skiani, whose comments on my earlier piece about waiting in AI products shaped most of this one, and who shared the production cases from Genie 007 quoted above.

Follow me on Medium for more essays on AI UX and the design reality of building for global audiences.

About the author: Adi Leviim is a full-stack engineer and product builder with 7+ years of experience shipping commercial software to global audiences. He writes about AI UX, the design reality of building for millions of users, and the gap between AI demos and production AI. Follow him on Medium for essays at the intersection of engineering and design.
